```{r options, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>", fig.width = 7,
                      fig.height = 4.5, fig.align = "center", dpi = 100)
```

The results of a network analysis are rarely limited to the network itself.
A report also ranks the nodes by centrality, shows how precisely each edge is
estimated, states which edges or nodes differ from one another, documents
whether the centrality order survives the loss of part of the sample, and,
when two groups are studied, tests whether their networks differ. Each of
these results is a distribution or a set of intervals, and each is read most
directly from a figure. A figure helps only if the reader knows what is
plotted against what, which marks denote significance, and what pattern would
support or undermine the conclusion.

This article draws the figure for each of these results from one network of
five self-regulated learning constructs, and states for each what it shows and
how to read it: centrality profiles, bootstrap intervals for edges and
centralities, difference matrices and forest plots, case-dropping stability
curves, and the permutation distributions of a network comparison test. All
figures are drawn by the `plot()` method of the corresponding result.

```{r setup}
library(psychnets)
```

## Data

`SRL_GPT` holds 300 sets of responses to the Motivated Strategies for Learning
Questionnaire, each a construct score on a scale from 1 to 7. The responses
were generated by a large language model (GPT) in a study of how such models
answer psychological surveys (Saqr, 2025). A second set, `SRL_Claude`, with
300 responses generated by another model, is the comparison group in the last
section.

- **Nodes:** `CSU` (cognitive strategy use), `IV` (intrinsic value), `SE`
  (self-efficacy), `SR` (self-regulation) and `TA` (test anxiety).
- **Observations:** one row per respondent; the data are complete.

```{r data}
head(SRL_GPT)
```

`ebic_glasso()` estimates the network whose results are drawn below: a
Gaussian graphical model whose edges are partial correlations selected by the
extended Bayesian information criterion.

```{r fit}
fit <- ebic_glasso(SRL_GPT)
fit
```

The network has 10 edges; the Gaussian graphical models article interprets
them.

## Which nodes are most central?

`net_centralities()` computes centrality measures, one row per node. Strength
is the sum of absolute edge weights, expected influence the signed sum, and
betweenness the proportion of shortest paths between other nodes that pass
through a node.

```{r centralities}
ct <- net_centralities(fit,
                       measures = c("strength", "expected_influence",
                                    "betweenness"))
ct
```

Self-regulation has the largest strength (1.231) and betweenness (0.5), but
its negative edge with test anxiety reduces its expected influence to 0.532,
below that of cognitive strategy use (1.198), intrinsic value (1.001) and
self-efficacy (0.849). Only cognitive strategy use and self-regulation lie on
shortest paths between other nodes. `plot()` draws one panel per measure,
with the nodes sorted by value so that the most central node is at the top:

```{r cent-bar, fig.width = 9, fig.height = 3.5}
plot(ct)
```

The three panels give three different orders, with self-regulation first on
strength and betweenness and fourth on expected influence. Which node is
"most central" depends on the measure, and a report names the measure.

## Do the nodes keep their position across measures?

With `type = "line"`, the nodes share one vertical order in all panels, set
by their mean standardized centrality, and each panel keeps its own axis. A
node whose line runs straight is equally central on every measure; a node
whose line bends is central on some measures and peripheral on others.

```{r cent-line, fig.width = 8, fig.height = 3.5}
plot(ct, type = "line")
```

The `scale` argument sets the transformation of each panel: `"raw"` (the
default) keeps the original values, `"z"` standardizes each measure to mean 0
and standard deviation 1, and `"relative"` rescales it to the range 0 to 1.
Standardized values put the three measures on one scale, so the bends become
comparable.

```{r cent-line-z, fig.width = 8, fig.height = 3.5}
plot(ct, type = "line", scale = "z")
```

Self-regulation bends most: high on strength and betweenness, low on expected
influence. Test anxiety is lowest on strength and expected influence.

## How precise are the edges?

`net_boot()` re-estimates the network on bootstrap samples of the
respondents and records every edge and centrality value; the percentile
interval of each is its measure of precision. An applied analysis uses at
least 1,000 samples; 250 keep this example short.

```{r boot}
set.seed(1)
bs <- net_boot(SRL_GPT, method = "glasso", n_boot = 250, cores = 1)
bs
```

Seven of the ten edges have 95% intervals that exclude zero. The default plot
shows each edge as its observed weight with its bootstrap interval, sorted by
weight. Edges whose interval excludes zero are drawn as filled points with
solid intervals, the others as open points with dashed intervals.

```{r boot-edges, fig.height = 5}
plot(bs)
```

The three edges whose intervals include zero are the small positive edges of
test anxiety with intrinsic value, self-efficacy and cognitive strategy use.
The negative self-regulation–test anxiety edge and the six edges among the
learning constructs are estimated with intervals that stay clear of zero.

## How precise is each node's centrality?

With `type = "centrality"`, the plot shows the bootstrap interval of each
node's centrality, one panel per measure.

```{r boot-cent}
plot(bs, type = "centrality")
```

```{r boot-cent-table}
as.data.frame(bs, what = "centrality")
```

The strength intervals of cognitive strategy use (1.08 to 1.35) and
self-regulation (1.08 to 1.36) almost coincide, so these two nodes cannot be
ordered on strength. Test anxiety (0.37 to 0.78) lies below every other node.
Wide and overlapping intervals are the visual signal that a ranking is
uncertain.

## Which edges and nodes differ from one another?

With `type = "edge_diff"` or `type = "centrality_diff"`, the plot shows a
matrix with the items on both axes, ordered from the largest to the smallest
observed value. The diagonal holds the observed values. An off-diagonal cell
is filled when the two items differ across the bootstrap samples, red when the
row item is larger and blue when it is smaller, and left faint otherwise;
stars give the p-value of the difference.

```{r boot-diff, fig.width = 6.5, fig.height = 6.5}
plot(bs, type = "edge_diff")
```

```{r boot-cent-diff, fig.width = 5.5, fig.height = 5.5}
plot(bs, type = "centrality_diff", measure = "strength")
```

The strength matrix shows which pairs of nodes can be ordered. The same
comparisons are available as a table from `difference_test()`, with the
observed difference, its interval, a p-value and a `significant` flag:

```{r difftest-tab}
dt <- difference_test(bs, type = "strength")
dt
```

Seven of the ten pairs differ. Test anxiety has lower strength than every
other node, self-regulation is stronger than intrinsic value and
self-efficacy, and cognitive strategy use is stronger than self-efficacy.
Three pairs cannot be ordered: cognitive strategy use and self-regulation
(difference -0.033, p = 0.712), cognitive strategy use and intrinsic value
(p = 0.080), and intrinsic value and self-efficacy (p = 0.208). A report can
place test anxiety last but should not name a single most central node.

`plot()` on the table draws the same matrix by default (`style = "box"`), which
shows *which* pairs differ.

```{r difftest-box, fig.width = 5.5, fig.height = 5.5}
plot(dt)
```

With `style = "forest"`, each pair is a row with its observed difference and
interval and a dashed line at zero, and pairs whose interval excludes zero
are emphasized. This view shows *how large* each difference is and how
uncertain.

```{r difftest-forest}
plot(dt, style = "forest")
```

## Is the centrality order stable when cases are dropped?

`net_stability()` re-estimates the network on subsets that drop an increasing
proportion of the respondents and correlates the subset centralities with
those of the full sample. The CS-coefficient is the largest proportion that
can be dropped while the correlation stays at or above 0.7 in at least 95% of
the subsets.

```{r stability-fit}
st <- net_stability(SRL_GPT, method = "glasso",
                    drop_prop = seq(0.1, 0.8, 0.1), iter = 25)
st
```

The CS-coefficient is 0.80 for both strength and expected influence, well
above the value of 0.5 recommended for interpreting centrality (Epskamp et
al., 2018). The plot shows the drop proportion on the horizontal axis and the
mean correlation with the full sample on the vertical axis, one line per
measure with a band of one standard deviation, and the threshold as a dashed
line. A curve that stays above the line as more cases are dropped indicates a
stable order.

```{r stability}
plot(st)
```

## Do the networks of two groups differ?

`net_compare()` performs the network comparison test (van Borkulo et al.,
2023). It reassigns the respondents of the two groups at random many times,
estimates both networks on each permutation, and compares the observed
differences with their distribution under random assignment. Two global
statistics are tested: M, network structure, the largest absolute difference
of any edge; and S, global strength, the difference in the sum of absolute
edge weights. Each edge is also tested separately.

```{r nct-fit}
cmp <- net_compare(SRL_GPT, SRL_Claude, iter = 250)
summary(cmp)
```

Both tests reject the hypothesis of equal networks (p = 0.004, the smallest
value possible with 250 permutations). The largest edge difference is 0.562,
and the global strength is 1.093 higher in the network of the Claude
responses (3.537 against 2.444). The default plot shows the permutation
distribution of S, with the observed value marked and the p-value in the
title; an observed value in the tail of the distribution is evidence of a
difference.

```{r nct}
plot(cmp)
```

The observed difference in global strength, 1.09, lies beyond every value in
the permutation distribution, which ends near 0.6.

With `type = "structure"`, the plot shows the same for M.

```{r nct-structure}
plot(cmp, type = "structure")
```

With `type = "edges"`, the plot shows the observed absolute difference of
each edge as a bar, coloured by whether the edge differs at `alpha`, and the
title gives the number of differing edges.

```{r nct-edges}
plot(cmp, type = "edges")
```

The per-edge results behind the bars, with the weight in each network, the
difference and its permutation p-value:

```{r nct-table}
as.data.frame(cmp)
```

Seven of the ten edges differ. The largest differences are `IV`–`SE` (0.160
against -0.402), `SE`–`TA` (0.099 against -0.418) and `CSU`–`TA` (0.049
against 0.526): the two sets of responses differ not only in how strongly the
constructs are related but in the sign of several relations.

## Summary of the plot methods

| Result (verb) | `plot()` options | Question |
|---|---|---|
| `net_centralities()` | `type = "bar"` / `"line"`; `scale = "raw"` / `"z"` / `"relative"` | Which nodes are central, on which measure? |
| `net_boot()` | `type = "edges"` / `"centrality"` / `"edge_diff"` / `"centrality_diff"` / `"predictability"` | How precise are edges and centralities, and which differ? |
| `difference_test()` | `style = "box"` / `"forest"` | Which pairs differ, and by how much? |
| `net_stability()` | one figure | Is the centrality order stable when cases are dropped? |
| `net_compare()` | `type = "strength"` / `"structure"` / `"edges"` | Do two networks differ? |

Each figure has a table behind it, read with the verb's own output or with
`as.data.frame()`, and reported values are taken from the table. The network
itself is drawn with `plot(fit)`, which uses the `cograph` package and is
covered in the article *Visualizing networks with cograph*.

## References

van Borkulo, C. D., van Bork, R., Boschloo, L., Kossakowski, J. J., Tio, P., Schoevers, R. A., Borsboom, D., & Waldorp, L. J. (2023). Comparing network structures on three aspects: A permutation test. *Psychological Methods*, 28(6), 1273-1285. [doi:10.1037/met0000476](https://doi.org/10.1037/met0000476)
